headline: From fire hazard to green gold
text:
Nepal’s forests are not only something to protect — managed well, they are a livelihood, a firebreak and a business at the same time.

1. A forest at risk

  • In Binayi Triveni, Nawalpur District, dry leaves, branches and undergrowth on the forest floor fed wildfires year after year.

  • Local women saw a resource where others saw a risk.

2. The enterprise

  • Meena Poudel, 41, Secretary of the Binayi Community Forest User Group, leads the collection.

  • The group composts that litter into organic fertiliser — “organically pure”, safer for the soil and for health.

3. The result

  • Forest fires fell by around 70% in a year.

  • What began as survival became stewardship — and a business built leaf by leaf.
media_caption: Meena Poudel and the Binayi Community Forest User Group collect forest biomass that once fed wildfires — now turned into organic fertiliser.

headline: Woodcarving empowers women
text:
Traditional craft plus business training can turn unpaid domestic work into an income — and turn a fire hazard into raw material.

1. The enterprise

  • Shramjivi Women Handicraft Enterprise, formed in 2017 in Piple-Pokhara, Makwanpur, works with soft wood and sawmill offcuts supplied by the Piple-Pokhara CFUG.

  • Because the raw material is forest litter that would otherwise burn, the craft also supports fire prevention.

2. What FFF support changed

  • October 2024 – October 2025: 15 women trained to make new products (Theki, wine glasses, bowls, trays, Okhal) and 10 women trained to professional carving level.

  • 30 women took part in business-plan and financial-literacy workshops.

  • Four community forests pledged raw material at reduced prices, and two local businesses — Bishwo Art and Hamro Printing Press — now stock the handicrafts.

3. The result

  • Women earn NPR 10,000–15,000 (USD 70–105) a month, selling locally, regionally and provincially.

  • Local government buys their handicrafts as gifts and tokens of appreciation.
media_caption: Woodcarving training with the Shramjivi Women Handicraft Enterprise, Piple-Pokhara, Makwanpur.

headline: Award-winning coffee transforms lives in Nepal
text:
Standards, nurseries and processing equipment are what turn a raw commodity into a branded product that pays better.

1. The union

  • Coffee Cooperative Union Limited (CCUL) has supported producers since 2012 and today covers 12 cooperatives with 473 members — over half women or youth, a quarter indigenous or Dalit.

  • Before FFF support, members depended on outside nurseries and roasters.

2. FFF support, 2024–25

  • Standard operating procedures for coffee production, processing and marketing, shared with every member.

  • Six nurseries established, targeting 50,000 seedlings a year.

  • A new roasting machine doubled the value of the coffee from USD 10 to USD 20 per kilogram, and members adopted coffee-based agroforestry with banana and Nepalese alder shade.

3. The result

  • The Beautiful Café in Sukute employs local women, and Sindu Organic Coffee is winning awards.

  • New domestic and international buyers are expanding the market.
media_caption: Coffee growers trained in post-harvest handling and climate-resilient techniques, Nepal.

headline: Turning leaves into livelihoods
text:
Appropriate technology, traditional knowledge and women-led enterprise can create income while supporting a cleaner, more sustainable environment.

1. The craft

  • For centuries women in Nepal have stitched Sal leaves with bamboo fibre into dunatapari — plates and bowls made from 2–12 leaves.

  • The 21 women of the Milijuli Tilakanya Dunatapri Udhyami Firm in Dangisharan earn their living from it.

2. The machine

  • An electricity-operated press using pressure and heat replaced a single-size machine that kept breaking down.

  • Output reached more than 108,000 plates in a year — three times the previous volume, in multiple sizes for hotels, weddings and family celebrations.

3. The result

  • Income of NPR 155,640 (USD 1,150) from a product that is 100% biodegradable.

  • With FFF support the cooperative lobbied local government, and single-use plastic utensils are now banned in Dangisharan and neighbouring Tulsipur.
media_caption: Sal leaf plates (dunatapari) produced by the Milijuli Tilakanya Dunatapri Udhyami Firm.

headline: From degraded lands to golden harvests
text:
Restoring degraded forest land and building a women-led enterprise do not have to be separate projects.

1. The problem

  • In 2022, forty women of the Bungdal Community Forest Group — over a third of them Tamang — were losing field crops to monkeys, porcupines and wild boar.

  • They formed Bungdal Mahila Aaye Aarjan Krishi Samuha and moved onto degraded community forest land.

2. Why turmeric

  • It is culturally significant and in demand, wildlife leave it alone because of its bitter taste, and it thrives in partial shade — so the community forest was the ideal plot.

  • The first agroforestry plot started with 8 quintals of rhizome, on soil rehabilitated with organic manure.

3. The result

  • 50 quintals harvested within two years — over six times the start.

  • Now around 20 quintals and NPR 275,000 (USD 2,040) a year, from a plot that restored 2.81 hectares of degraded land.

  • FFF support covered training (including the Kapurkot Haledo 1 and 2 varieties, and drying instead of boiling for higher curcumin), the Enterprise Development Plan endorsed by the forest general assembly, and market links.
media_caption: Women of the Bungdal Mahila Aaye Aarjan Krishi Samuha growing turmeric in the community forest.

headline: Revitalized allo enterprise empowers women
text:
An ancestral craft can become a modern business when the women who hold the skill also hold the machine, the market and the plan.

1. The craft

  • Allo, the Himalayan giant nettle, grows up to three metres tall. Its fibres are harvested by hand, then washed, boiled, pounded and dried over months before being spun and woven.

  • The skill has passed down generations of indigenous women — it is traditionally their domain.

2. Near collapse

  • After the pandemic the Risheshwor Allo Enterprise in Makwanpur was running at a loss: a worn-out machine and thread-only production, with no skills for value-added products.

  • “Our enterprise was underperforming,” says Hira Lama, Chairperson. “It was a very difficult time for us.”

3. The turnaround

  • FFF-supported workshops in 2024 brought pledges of reduced-price raw material from four community forests, and the Risheshwor Community Forest planted over 3,200 allo plants — restoration and supply at once.

  • New processing equipment, and an exposure visit to Allo Bazar Pvt Ltd that taught the women to make coats, bags and shoes.

  • Linked to SABHA Nepal market outlets and promoted on community FM and social media — income has almost doubled. The enterprise now has 7 workers, 7 executive members and 2 advisors.
media_caption: Allo fibre being washed and dried before spinning, Risheshwor Allo Enterprise, Makwanpur.
